Reviews likewise frame SV2B as an emerging candidate rather than an established epilepsy gene (PMID 27752944). This profile best fits "Hypothesized."

The remaining literature is largely pharmacological/review material (PMIDs 24896213, 9757152, 9357097) showing CYP3A4 biology is relevant to epilepsy therapy, which would only support "Hypothesized".

justification: All the EPHX1 papers here are pharmacogenetic: EPHX1 c.337T>C and c.416A>G influence carbamazepine metabolism, dose requirements and plasma CBZ/CBZ-epoxide ratios in epilepsy patients (PMIDs 19620853, 24125961, 25495409, 26555147, 22188362, 27276192), carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN risk (24861996), and phenytoin-related congenital malformations (19952982). No study in this set reports EPHX1 variants as a cause of, or susceptibility factor for, epilepsy itself; in the one study examining epilepsy susceptibility, the association was with SCN1A, not EPHX1 (26555147), and EPHX1 was explicitly not associated with pharmacoresistance (24125961, 26555147). One paper (24817818) even failed to replicate an effect on CBZ-epoxide levels in vivo. Thus the evidence supports a drug-metabolism/mechanistic link in epilepsy patients rather than a genetic cause of the disease; "Established" is excluded since no two studies report EPHX1 variants causing epilepsy in independent probands or families.

justification: The strongest evidence linking CAMK2A to epilepsy is non-human: αCaMKII null mutant mice develop spontaneous limbic seizures (PMID 7624331), antisense knockdown of αCaMKII in cultured hippocampal neurons produces epileptiform discharges (PMID 10779547), and seizure models show altered Camk2a expression (PMIDs 24282673, 19446251, 26670047). These provide a compelling biological/mechanistic rationale but no human variant data for epilepsy. The only human CAMK2A variant studies concern ASD (de novo E183V, PMID 28130356), bipolar disorder rare variants (PMID 25730879), conduct disorder and Alzheimer-related polymorphisms, none of which report epilepsy phenotypes; the 5q32 deletions (PMID 23695276) are multigenic CNVs with intellectual disability, not epilepsy, and cannot isolate CAMK2A. Many other papers merely use the CaMKIIα promoter as a transgenic driver (PMIDs 10103085, 11248115, 22158510, 23143518), which is an incidental co-mention. Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with a small allowance for "existing" based on the ASD/neurodevelopmental human variant data as a loosely related mechanism.

justification: The only human study whose own results link GRM8 variants to epilepsy is the targeted resequencing "Astrochip" study (PMID 26537360), where predicted-deleterious/non-coding GRM8 variants clustered with the autism-epilepsy phenotype subgroup — suggestive but far from definitive and not replicated. The remainder of the supportive evidence is pharmacological/animal: mGluR8 agonists (DCPG, 3,4-DCPG) are anticonvulsant in DBA/2 mice, mGluR8 modulates perforant path and piriform cortex transmission in epilepsy models, and reviews list mGluR8 as an epilepsy drug target (PMIDs 11311902, 15152022, 18625254, 23220400, 25506748) — strong biological plausibility but no human variant causality. No two independent human studies with single-gene variants in epilepsy probands exist, so Established is excluded.

justification: Human association data exist: the EPIGEN multicentre candidate-gene study flagged SYN2 among the top loci in set-association analyses (PMID 17913586), a North Indian case-control study reported association of SYN2 rs3773364 with idiopathic epilepsy (PMID 20034013), and a South Indian study reported association of a SYN2 intronic variant with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (PMID 25088614). Strong supportive biology comes from mouse knockouts with seizures and impaired GABAergic transmission (PMIDs 7777057, 21281619, 22236379, 28087765, 24227741), which supports plausibility but is non-human. Therefore "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" if one discounts the small, non-replicated human association studies.

Some uncertainty remains because the Karaca report is a broad candidate-gene discovery study with limited phenotypic detail, and the 4p16.3 deletion work (PMID 24738919) implicates a multigene region rather than CPLX1 specifically; other papers concern schizophrenia or Parkinson's disease and are not relevant to epilepsy causation. justification: None of the provided articles mention epilepsy, seizures, or any human genetic study of VTI1A variants in patients, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported (no probands, families, or association studies are reported). The literature instead characterizes vti1a as a neuronal SNARE enriched in small synaptic vesicles and clathrin-coated vesicles at nerve terminals (PMID 10908612), involved in dense-core vesicle biogenesis and Ca2+-channel trafficking in chromaffin cells (PMID 24902738), and in a VAMP7/Vti1a complex required for surface trafficking of KChIP1/Kv4 potassium channels in neuronal cells (PMID 19138172). Remaining human genetic associations for SLC6A13 concern renal function and serum metabolites (PMIDs 21931561, 24311711, 24625756), unrelated to epilepsy. justification: Two human reports implicate CACNA2D1 in epilepsy: three patients with genomic aberrations of CACNA2D1 presenting with epilepsy and intellectual disability (PMID 25074461), and a trio exome study identifying a de novo CACNA2D1 mutation as a candidate gene in unexplained West syndrome (PMID 25877686). Other human CACNA2D1 variant reports concern cardiac phenotypes (short QT, Brugada; PMIDs 21383000, 20817017), which are not epilepsy precursors. Overall this best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the reliance on animal/functional data.
